# One Seed, Many Keys

A FOKS device needs several different keys. It signs chain links, so it needs
a signature key. It receives encrypted key material from other devices, so it
needs a key-agreement key and, because the design is post-quantum, a second
key for a lattice-based key encapsulation mechanism. It encrypts small
records for itself, so it needs a symmetric key. Storing four independent
secrets would multiply every problem that comes with secret storage: backup,
transfer between machines, zeroization, and the accounting of which secret
belongs to which purpose.

FOKS stores one 32-byte secret per key-bearing party and derives everything
else from it. This chapter explains the derivation technique in general, then
shows how `foks-rs` uses it to produce a device's *key suite*, how public
keys become identifiers, and how a single 64-bit *type ID* is threaded
through every hash, MAC, signature, and nonce in the protocol so that no two
objects can be confused for one another.

## Key derivation from a master secret

A *pseudorandom function* (PRF) is a keyed function whose outputs, to anyone
who does not know the key, are indistinguishable from random. Given a PRF
$F$ and a master secret $s$, the value $F(s, \text{label})$ is a fresh secret
that reveals nothing about $s$ and nothing about $F(s, \text{label}')$ for any
other label. That single property is enough to fan one secret out into as
many as needed: choose a distinct label for each purpose.

HMAC (RFC 2104) is the usual choice of PRF. It takes a key and a message and
returns a fixed-size tag, and its security as a PRF rests on the compression
function of the underlying hash. With HMAC over SHA-512/256 the output is 32
bytes, which is exactly the size FOKS wants for every derived secret.

The one thing that can go wrong is label ambiguity. If two callers can
produce the same label bytes for different purposes, they get the same
derived key. The labels must therefore be encoded so that distinct meanings
give distinct byte strings. FOKS solves this with the same canonical encoding
it uses on the wire (see [Chapter 9](09-canonical-encoding.qmd)).

The better-known HKDF (RFC 5869) is a two-step construction: an *extract*
step condenses input keying material of uncertain quality into a uniform key,
and an *expand* step produces output of any length. FOKS does not need the
extract step, because its seeds are already uniformly random, and it never
needs more than 32 bytes at a time. The repository's own guide describes
`derive_key` as an "HKDF hierarchy"; the code is a single keyed HMAC call
with a typed label. The two are related in spirit but are not the same
function, and outputs are not interchangeable.

## `derive_key`

Every software key in FOKS (a device key, a per-user key, a per-team key, a
backup key, a passphrase key, a bot token, a delegated subkey) is a
`SecretSeed`: 32 bytes held in zeroizing storage and redacted from debug
output. The function that fans a seed out is:

```
derive_key(seed, t, i) =
    HMAC-SHA-512/256( key = seed,
                      msg = BE64(0xd35c_dcc9_5cae_f674) || encode([t, i]) )
```

`BE64(x)` is the eight-byte big-endian encoding of `x`; the constant is the
type ID reserved for key derivation. `encode([t, i])` is the canonical
Snowpack encoding of a two-element list: the derivation type `t`, and either
an empty variant (when no index is needed) or a variant tagged `4` carrying
the index `i`. The derivation types the Rust code uses are:

| `t` | Index | Derived secret | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | none | Ed25519 signing seed | identity and all signatures |
| 1 | none | X25519 static secret | classical half of hybrid encryption |
| 2 | none | 32-byte symmetric key | secretboxes keyed by a seed (seed chains, passphrase parcels, hardware-key escrow, federation tokens) |
| 4 | 0 and 1 | two 32-byte halves | concatenated into the 64-byte ML-KEM-768 seed |
| 5 | none | application-key root | key-value store and chat keys (see [Chapter 5](05-generations.qmd)) |

Type 3 does not appear in the Rust code. The ML-KEM case is the only one that
needs an index: FIPS 203 defines key generation from a pair of 32-byte
values $(d, z)$, and the `ml-kem` crate takes them as one 64-byte seed, so
FOKS derives each half separately and joins them.

Because derivation is deterministic, whoever holds a seed can reconstruct
the entire suite at any time. This is what makes the recovery phrase in
[Chapter 6](06-hesp.qmd) sufficient on its own: the phrase encodes one seed,
and everything else follows from it.

## The device key suite

From a device seed the suite is:

| Component | Derived from | Public form | Size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ed25519 signing key | `derive_key(seed, 0)` | verify key | 32 bytes |
| X25519 static key | `derive_key(seed, 1)` | X25519 public key | 32 bytes |
| ML-KEM-768 key pair | `derive_key(seed, 4, 0) ‖ derive_key(seed, 4, 1)` | encapsulation key | 1184 bytes |

The verify key becomes the device's identifier (next section). The X25519
public key and the ML-KEM encapsulation key are packaged together as a
*hybrid encryption public key* (HEPK), the object [Chapter 4](04-hybrid-encryption.qmd)
is about. Chain links carry only a 32-byte typed hash of the HEPK, called its
fingerprint, and the full key (about 1.2 kB encoded) is uploaded alongside
and checked against that fingerprint.

The same Ed25519 key does one more job. `foks-rs` talks to servers over
mutually authenticated TLS, and the client certificate is signed with the
device's own signing key. The code wraps the 32-byte Ed25519 seed in a
hand-built PKCS#8 header (the RFC 8410 form that TLS libraries expect), so a
device authenticates to the transport with the same key that authenticates
its chain links. There is no separate transport identity to provision or
revoke.

## Entity IDs

Every party that holds keys has an *entity ID*: one type byte followed by a
public key. For software keys the public key is the 32-byte Ed25519 verify
key, so the ID is 33 bytes. For a hardware key (see
[Chapter 7](07-hardware-keys.qmd)) it is a 33-byte compressed P-256 point, so
the ID is 34 bytes. The type bytes in use are:

| Type byte | Entity |
|---|---|
| 1 | user |
| 2 | host |
| 3 | named team |
| 4 | device |
| 8 | YubiKey (hardware device) |
| 10 | host Merkle signer |
| 11 | host TLS certificate authority |
| 12 | host metadata signer |
| 13 | delegated subkey |
| 14 | per-user key (PUK) verify key |
| 15 | per-team key (PTK) verify key |
| 16 | backup key |
| 17 | passphrase key |
| 19 | bot token key |
| 20 | ad hoc team |

The type byte is not decoration. Functions that expect a host ID call
`require_type(ENTITY_HOST)` and refuse anything else, and the signature
verifier dispatches on it: type 8 must carry an ECDSA signature, every other
type must carry Ed25519. Two parties with the same underlying public key but
different type bytes are different entities.

The most instructive consequence is how users and teams get their IDs. A
user ID is the first owner per-user key's verify key with the type byte
overwritten: the code copies the 33-byte PUK verify key and sets byte 0 to 1.
A team ID is likewise the initial admin per-team key's verify key with byte 0
set to 3 (named team) or 20 (ad hoc team). Identifiers are therefore
*self-certifying*: the party that generated the first key chose the ID, the
ID commits to a public key that only the key holder can use, and a server
that wanted to substitute a different identity would have to produce a
different ID. The server assigns nothing.

## Type IDs: domain separation everywhere

*Domain separation* is the practice of making sure that a cryptographic
function applied for one purpose can never produce an output that is valid
for another purpose. The classic failure is a signature over raw bytes: if a
chain link and, say, a Merkle root could be serialized to the same bytes, a
signature on one would verify as a signature on the other. Fixing such
collisions one at a time is error-prone. FOKS fixes them systematically.

Every protocol object type has a 64-bit constant called its type ID. A few
of the ones that appear in this part of the book:

| Constant | Value | Object |
|---|---|---|
| `LINK_OUTER_V1_TYPE_ID` | `0xc274_5284_af61_7745` | signed chain link |
| `SHARED_KEY_SEED_TYPE_ID` | `0xa999_8e7a_59e8_ae25` | boxed PUK/PTK seed |
| `HEPK_TYPE_ID` | `0x9c58_1bee_d36c_7e0c` | hybrid public key fingerprint |
| `HYBRID_SECRET_KEY_SHA3_PAYLOAD_TYPE_ID` | `0x8a9e_3276_4726_2289` | hybrid key combiner |
| `TEMP_DH_KEY_SIG_TEMPLATE_TYPE_ID` | `0xd51b_5d99_0285_023e` | temporary DH key signature |
| `BACKUP_SEED_TYPE_ID` | `0xf4c4_fe8d_ff61_a6dc` | recovery-kit seed hash |
| `KEX_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID` | `0x8d7b_c770_3f63_ad64` | pairing-code key derivation |
| `KEX_CLEARTEXT_TYPE_ID` | `0xd2bc_e826_3ea1_dc0b` | pairing packet secretbox |
| `NAME_COMMITMENT_TYPE_ID` | `0xe37b_1fcf_ba97_2353` | username commitment |
| `DEVICE_LABEL_TYPE_ID` | `0x9650_2272_0548_6122` | device-name commitment |
| `APP_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID` | `0x9431_8317_830b_409b` | application key root |
| `KV_KEY_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID` | `0xdbdf_2ba2_9c0d_e2cb` | key-value store keys |

The type ID is prepended, big-endian, to the canonical encoding of an object
before the object is hashed, signed, MACed, or encrypted. Four operations
share this layout:

- **Typed hash.** `prefixed_hash(T, obj) = SHA-512/256(BE64(T) ‖ obj)`. The
  variant used for protocol objects, `prefixed_hash_signable`, first checks
  that `obj` is a valid canonical encoding, so only one byte string per
  object is ever hashed.
- **Typed signature.** Ed25519 signs `BE64(T) ‖ obj` directly. For P-256
  (hardware keys) the same message is first reduced with SHA-512/256, because
  the card signs a 32-byte digest.
- **Typed HMAC.** `typed_hmac(k, T, obj) = HMAC-SHA-512/256(k, BE64(T) ‖ obj)`,
  used for key derivation, commitments, and the integrity bindings of the
  key-value store.
- **Typed nonce.** NaCl secretboxes take a 24-byte nonce. FOKS fills the
  first 8 bytes with the type ID and the remaining 16 with random bytes (or a
  value derived from the object's identity). A ciphertext produced for one
  purpose cannot be opened under another purpose even with the same key,
  because the nonce would differ.

The cost is eight bytes per object. In return, the space of things that can
collide shrinks to objects of the same declared type, and for those the
canonical encoding guarantees a unique representation.

Type IDs are random 64-bit values, so they need no central registry. When
the Rust implementation needs a new local domain that will never appear on
the wire, it allocates one by hashing a descriptive label: the chat-v2 module
takes the first eight bytes of SHA-256 over the ASCII strings
`foks.chat.v2.context-key` and `foks.chat.v2.encrypted-body`, and comments
that these are not upstream Go IDs. The probability that a label-derived ID
collides with an existing one is negligible, and the label is a permanent
record of what the ID means.

The same idea is standardised in NIST SP 800-185 as TupleHash and cSHAKE
customization strings; FOKS's layout is simpler but serves the same purpose.

## Commitments

A *commitment* is a value that binds its author to some data without
revealing it. It has two properties: *hiding* (the commitment alone reveals
nothing about the data) and *binding* (once published, it cannot be opened
to different data). The HMAC of the data under a fresh random key is a
commitment: without the key the tag reveals nothing, and finding a second
input with the same tag under the same key would break HMAC.

FOKS uses commitments where a chain must record a fact without publishing
it. Usernames and device names are not written into chain links in the
clear. Instead the link carries

```
commitment = HMAC-SHA-512/256( key = 16 random bytes,
                               msg = BE64(NAME_COMMITMENT_TYPE_ID) ‖ encode([name, sequence]) )
```

and the 16-byte key is disclosed only to parties that are allowed to learn
the name. Device labels use the same construction under
`DEVICE_LABEL_TYPE_ID`. A verifier that has both the key and the name can
check the link; anyone else sees an opaque 32-byte value.

Two more commitments are worth knowing about because they shape
[Part III](10-sigchains.qmd). Each chain link commits to the Merkle-tree
location of the *next* link as `prefixed_hash_signable(TREE_LOCATION_TYPE_ID, bin(location))`,
so the server cannot choose where the next link lands. And a user's or team's
subchain starts at a hidden location derived from the seed,
`HMAC-SHA-512/256(seed, BE64(CHAIN_LOCATION_DERIVATION_TYPE_ID) ‖ encode([chain_type, {}]))`,
so an observer of the tree cannot tell which leaves belong to which party
without the seed.

## Why this design

The seed-and-derive structure trades one risk for several conveniences. The
risk is concentration: a single 32-byte value is the whole device, so the
places it lives (the local keystore of [Chapter 8](08-local-keystore.qmd),
the recovery kit of [Chapter 6](06-hesp.qmd)) carry the full weight of the
design. The conveniences are that there is exactly one thing to back up, one
thing to transfer, one thing to zeroize; that derivation is cheap enough to
repeat on every use rather than caching derived keys on disk; and that
adding a new purpose is a matter of choosing a new derivation type.

The choice of a single HMAC over HKDF, and of SHA-512/256 over SHA-256, is
compatibility: the reference Go implementation made these choices and
`foks-rs` must produce byte-identical keys from the same seed. The typed
layout for hashes, signatures, MACs, and nonces was also inherited, and it is
the part of the design that generalises best. Any protocol that signs more
than one kind of object should do something like it.

## Where to look

- `foks-crypto` (`crates/foks-crypto/src/lib.rs`): `derive_key`,
  `derive_mlkem_seed`, `derive_public_material`, `device_signing_key_pkcs8`,
  `prefixed_hash`, `prefixed_hash_signable`, `typed_hmac`, `commitment`,
  `sign_ed25519_typed`, `verify_typed`, `seal_typed_secretbox`,
  `subchain_tree_location`.
- `foks-crypto` (`account.rs`, `chat_v2.rs`): username commitments and
  label-derived local type IDs.
- `foks-proto` (`lib.rs`, `entity.rs`, `key_material.rs`,
  `identity/hepk.rs`): type ID and entity-type constants, `EntityId`,
  `SecretSeed`, `Hepk`.
- `foks-snowpack`: the canonical encoding that makes derivation labels and
  hashed objects unambiguous.
